title: Trial by fire – and flood: A new chief pursues FEMA reforms
text:
Trial by fire – and flood: A new chief pursues FEMA reforms
Cam Hamilton faces a test as the new Federal Emergency Management Agency head, addressing rising needs while letting local responders take the lead.
A fourth-generation military service member and former Navy SEAL combat medic, Cam Hamilton knows something about improvising – and surviving – under stress. After four overseas tours, he joined the nation’s Homeland Security office, where he oversaw nearly 4,000 emergency responders.
Those instincts and acumen will be vital in his new role as head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, America’s struggling disaster-response corps. It’s not just that the number of major natural disasters has been growing. There has also been a policy storm around the agency’s size and mission.
At the start of his second term, President Donald Trump threatened to close the agency altogether, then reduced its staffing by almost 20% and froze or clawed back billions in funding, joining a growing chorus of critics who said FEMA had become bloated and ineffective. The goal, he said, was to make FEMA more state partner than single-stop responder.
Former U.S. Navy SEAL Cam Hamilton is stepping in with the goal of reforming the nation’s disaster response agency – a mission that affects the safety and well-being of communities across the country.
Now Mr. Hamilton, a MAGA-aligned Republican who was sworn in Aug. 10, has the opportunity to shift disaster response back to its roots: providing a strong federal partner to support a strengthened local response. Whether he can achieve effective reform and responsiveness simultaneously remains to be seen. But as states keep guard against Atlantic hurricanes and the most destructive wildfire season in a decade, it’s significant that FEMA has its first permanent administrator in over a year and a half.
“Cam Hamilton seems to be nationally where the public is,” says Christopher Cooper, a political scientist at Western Carolina University in Cullowhee, N.C. “He doesn’t want to kill FEMA. But he does want to reform FEMA.”
Reforms are difficult, says Julian Muhammad, the interim director of North Carolina Central University’s Institute for Homeland Security and Emergency Management in Durham, because many states have become overreliant on federal aid. That sense of FEMA aid as an entitlement, he says, has hobbled efforts to mitigate against disasters to reduce response costs.
Critics say that the administration’s approach has led to widened disparities in emergency capacity across states, influenced by partisan politics and uneven state-level resources.
But Mr. Hamilton’s defense of FEMA’s mission while pushing reforms has already earned him bipartisan support.
“There’s genuine willingness and excitement to work with him from across the political spectrum,” says Andrew Rumbach, senior fellow at the Urban Institute. “He’s walking a tightrope ... [but] people want reform, and he has an opportunity to lead the reform.”
A backlog of “billion-dollar disasters”
FEMA, which often experiences understaffing and an overload of cases, especially during seasons of high disaster activity or changes in administrations, is currently struggling to process funding for hundreds of communities nationwide, with an unusually large backlog of over 700 open or active recovery projects.
Costs have also ratcheted up – a fact that intensifies the debate around FEMA’s performance, given the jump in the raw number of what the federal government calls “billion-dollar disasters’’ from two major storm events in 2004 to 17 in 2024. Some of the most recent: Super Typhoon Bavi hitting the Northern Mariana Islands; historic floods in Indiana; and a major wildfire near Reno, Nevada.
On Sept. 10, Mr. Hamilton toured areas near Spokane, Washington, struck by wildfires in August. He met with faith leaders and over 20 tribal leaders. He promised the federal government would streamline, not complicate, recovery efforts, and said that such reforms are “critical because it will drive these communities’ economic interests while helping them be more resilient than before.”
Who’s in charge, and what are the rules?
After Mr. Trump repeatedly called on Congress to abolish it, the FEMA Review Council in March set out new recommendations aimed at shifting more responsibility to states, setting new disaster-declaration limits, and reducing funding. But the council acknowledged that Congress will have to approve any fundamental reforms.
Yet for all those swirling dynamics, “nothing has changed about FEMA’s mission – zero,” says Christopher Currie, a director with Congress’ nonpartisan Government Accountability Office. “So if another big event happens anywhere in the country” – from Puerto Rico to Guam, he says, noting the agency’s reach – “it has to mount an effective response.”
That, by many accounts, has become tougher, resulting in bog downs on the ground.
An August GAO report found that the agency lost 1 in 6 employees in the last year, many of whom were senior in rank. FEMA went from 25,134 employees in 2025 to fewer than 20,000 now – over a 17% reduction.
“The agency lost a tremendous amount of capacity,” says Mr. Rumbauch at the Urban Institute. Staff cuts driven by the Department of Government Efficiency were “not well thought out” and have hurt FEMA morale, he says.
Moreover, the days between a disaster and a presidential emergency declaration have been growing in the last 10 years. An analysis by The New York Times this spring showed that disaster money is flowing more slowly to the states that Mr. Trump lost in the 2024 election.
The White House has insisted that “there is no politicization to the President’s decisions on disaster relief.” Mr. Rumbauch says he’s also hesitant to paint the process as political, given the many dynamics that go into a declaration, including those made by other administrations.
Nevertheless, “there is a sense that it is partisan politics playing a role” in disaster declarations and staffing cuts, says Professor Muhammad in North Carolina. “You have diminished capabilities even as disasters are becoming more frequent and catastrophic.”
FEMA’s press office declined to make Mr. Hamilton or any other officials available for an interview requested by the Monitor.
Aid appears to have been more forthcoming under the leadership of the new Homeland Security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, who replaced Kristi Noem as head of the Department of Homeland Security (which includes FEMA ) earlier this year. Ms. Noem had put into place several budgetary rules that critics claimed slowed the agency’s response time.
And the agency pushed back on the GAO’s critical report, noting that “current staffing levels remain robust, with more than 19,800 deployable personnel – the highest number of deployable staff since 2016.”
“We’re ensuring workforce stability and a strong, deployable force for upcoming national events and potential disasters,” the unsigned statement said, all while “making the agency leaner, faster and laser-focused on supporting state, local, tribal and territorial partners before, during and after disasters.”
A full roster of challenges
Mr. Hamilton’s challenges are both political and practical. He has said he wants to shore up aging information technology systems, streamline individual aid, and safeguard against fraud and waste.
He has also traveled a tumultuous path to becoming FEMA’s administrator. Mr. Hamilton briefly led the agency from January to May 2025, but was fired by Ms. Noem after he publicly contradicted Mr. Trump’s statement that the agency should be abolished.
After his dismissal, Mr. Hamilton kept up his critiques, being careful not to single out Mr. Trump.
“FEMA is saving money, which is good due to the astronomical US debt from Congress,” he wrote on the social platform X after his dismissal. “Despite this, FEMA staff are responding to entirely new forms of bureaucracy ... that is lengthening wait times for claim recipients, and delaying the deployment of time-sensitive resources.”
In part, his return underscores a broader sense that, for all its flaws, FEMA remains a key agency in need of leadership.
In disaster-struck rural places such as “western North Carolina, there’s a sense that the government failed the people of [the region], and that’s a feeling they’ve had for a long time,” says Dr. Cooper, in Cullowhee.
